# Probability-integral residuals

A Pearson plot of a binary or a count fit is striped. The stripes are the values the response is allowed to take, not a missed term. This is the last diagnostic that still belongs with generalised linear models. It replaces that plot with a transform that does not care what the distribution was.

Suppose $Y$ has continuous distribution function $F$. Then $U=F(Y)$ is uniform on $(0,1)$. The probability of falling below the value you actually observed, scored by the distribution that generated it, is a uniform draw. If $F$ is discrete the same idea uses a generalised inverse, and $F(Y)$ is only approximately uniform. The approximation improves as the fitted distribution spreads over more values. A Bernoulli is the worst case. A Poisson with a large mean is kinder.

After a model has been fitted, plug in $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ and compute $F(y_i;\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})$ for each observation. These are not exactly uniform, for the same reason a residual divided by $\hat\sigma$ is not exactly standard normal: the parameters were estimated. If the model is adequate they should still look like a uniform sample. Order them and plot them against the uniform quantiles $1/n,2/n,\ldots,n/n$. Those quantiles are equally spaced, which is the one pleasant feature of the uniform that the normal does not share. A straight line is what you want.

::: {.callout-note}
## Key idea
A probability-integral residual asks whether each observation sits where the fitted distribution said it would. The reference distribution is uniform, for a binomial, a Poisson, a gamma, or a normal. You do not first transform the data toward normality.
:::

Bend the line and the fit is wrong in a readable way. If the plotted residuals bow above the diagonal through the middle of the sample, the middle observations are larger than the fitted distribution expected: the mean is too low in the middle of the range. The opposite bow means the fit is too high there. Either shape is a reason to change the mean, not to stare harder at a banded Pearson plot.

![Left: probability-integral residuals from the gamma clotting fit, plotted against equally spaced uniform quantiles. The dashed line is what an adequate fit looks like; eighteen points still wiggle around it. Right: the bow described above, not a fit to a data set. Above the diagonal through the middle means the middle observations are larger than the fitted distribution expected.](../figures/pit.pdf){#fig-pit}

The same construction works when the data really are normal. $F$ is then a normal distribution function, and the uniform plot is that normal probability transformed one more time. The classical residual plots remain the right tool when $Y$ is continuous and the variance function is the thing in doubt.

The next question is what to do when no straight line, on any link, is a shape you are willing to write down in advance.

## Exercises

1. State what $F(Y)$ is distributed as when $F$ is the true continuous distribution function of $Y$, and why the plotted reference quantiles for a sample of size $n$ are equally spaced.
